title: Temporal Ruptures in Post-World War II French Autofiction
content: This article examines temporal ruptures in postwar French autofiction and related autobiographical writing through four works: Marguerite Duras’s La Douleur (1985), Georges Perec’s W ou le souvenir d’enfance (1975), Serge Doubrovsky’s Fils (1977), and Annie Ernaux’s Les Années (2008). It asks when a return, omission, pause, repetition, or shift in time changes how a past event reaches the present. The comparison traces four approaches: waiting that holds an outcome open, montage that sets personal memories beside public traces, shifts between autobiographical and fictional stories, and narration that draws attention to the making of the self. These approaches do not describe one shared experience of trauma. Duras and Perec write directly about wartime violence and loss. Ernaux places personal memory within French social history. Doubrovsky examines remembered identity through psychoanalysis and language. Close readings show that breaks in time can make uncertainty and the limits of memory visible, but can also obscure context or make testimony harder to follow. Their ethical effect depends on what each work makes clear and what it leaves out.
